newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian PM, finance minister hint at oil-price rise.
newsitem.headline: Indian PM, finance minister hint at oil-price rise.

text.p: India's Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda and Finance Minister P. Chidambaram, though clearly wary of upsetting coalition partners, have both hinted that a rise in subsidised oil prices was inevitable.

"At least somebody is telling the truth," Deve Gowda remarked to reporters on Friday night, referring to comments last November by Manmohan Singh, former finance minister in the previous Congress Party government, that a rise in domestic oil prices was inevitable.

Government ministers have been saying for months that India needs to increase petroleum product prices to reflect a steep rise in world prices in the past six months, but coalition partners have resisted.

"I cannot alone say anything. The cabinet has to decide," Deve Gowda said, alluding to the constraints of working within a 13-party coalition which combines centrist, communists, farmer and regional parties.
The government depends on support from the Congress Party, which remains outside the coalition, and Singh's comments have encouraged those in government favouring an oil price rise.

Chidambaram on Thursday told communist members of the United Front government's steering committee, which double-checks policy decision-making, that he would take into account their objections to any oil price hikes -- without saying what policy option he would eventually take.
The United Front coalition raised fuel product prices by an average 15 percent last July after just a month in office, leading to protests from the opposition in parliament.

The move followed two years of inaction by the Congress Party to reduce a deficit in the oil pool account, which is the amount the government owes India's oil companies for selling petroleum products to Indian consumers below world prices.
Crude oil prices were around $17 a barrel at the time of the last Indian price rise and have since risen past $25, Deve Gowda pointed out.
On Friday North Sea crude fell below $23 for the first time this year, on hopes that warmer weather in the northern hemisphere would bring further relief in the coming months.
In the meantime, India is wading through a quagmire of budget troubles and the creditworthiness of Indian oil companies is worsening.

The oil companies sell products at low subsidised prices and claim back the difference between market prices from the oil pool account -- but the companies have to borrow from banks to meet operational costs while they wait to be reimbursed.
The Oil Coordination Committee, which oversees India's administered pricing mechanism, says the oil pool deficit will reach 155 billion rupees ($4.3 billion) in March this year.
The issue is heating up ahead of the start of discussions next month on India's budget for the 1997/98 financial year.

The Economic Times newspaper on Saturday reported that government budget proposals which have Congress Party support would free diesel and liquified petroleum gas prices, the first steps in dismantling the pricing regime.
On Wednesday, Deve Gowda responded to questions about how the oil pool account would be funded by saying, "For the time being, the only thing is borrowings itself."

That fuelled speculation that the government was going to avoid a price rise, leaving oil companies under pressure while ducking the inflationary impact and protecting industry and consumers from higher world prices.
But in light of his comments on Friday, it now appears that Gowda meant that deficit finance borrowing would continue until the cabinet decided whether to raise prices.

Meanwhile, Chidambaram, while accepting communist calls for the government to borrow for the oil pool account rather than inflict another price rise on the public, warned that deficit financing was "not always desirable".
